CANONICAL_NAME.value: 4.2BSD TCP (1983) -- the pre-congestion-control TCP that collapsed the Internet in 1986

value.lineage: TCP congestion-control lineage, the KNOWN-BAD ancestor: 4.2BSD's TCP (Bill Joy, Sam Leffler) had retransmission timers and windows but NO congestion window, NO slow start and a crude RTT estimate. In October 1986 the LBL-to-Berkeley path fell from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s -- congestion collapse -- which is the pressure that produced 4.3BSD-Tahoe's algorithms (Jacobson 1988). Preserved from the unix-history-repo (Spinellis) at tag BSD-4_2.

value.built_to: deliver a reliable byte stream over an unreliable internet using windows and retransmission timers
value.pressure: packet loss and delay from shared links; but the design did not yet read loss as a congestion signal
value.success_means: data arrives in order; when the network is congested this version keeps retransmitting into it -- the human record marks that as its failure

value.pressure: bandwidth scarcity on shared links, packet loss, queueing delay
value.failure_condition: congestion collapse: throughput falls by three orders of magnitude while every host keeps retransmitting

evidence.ref: Jacobson & Karels, Congestion Avoidance and Control, SIGCOMM 1988
evidence.says: In October 1986 the LBL-to-Berkeley path collapsed from 32 kbit/s to 40 bit/s; the paper attributes this to TCP lacking congestion control and introduces slow start and congestion avoidance as the fix.
